display_name: Lafage Tessellae Old Vines, Côtes du Roussillon
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "Tessellae Old Vines is a Côtes du Roussillon red built from low-yield, old-vine fruit with a Mediterranean imprint: hot, dry summers, the drying Tramontane wind and soils of schist, granite and limestone across the appellation. That combination concentrates dark fruit and savory, mineral tannins — a workhorse Roussillon red that trades high-octane ripeness for layered, terroir-driven weight.",
  "wine_summary": "This bottling matters because it channels the identity of Côtes du Roussillon — sun-ripe Grenache/Carignan-driven character (grape varieties are not specified on the label) tempered by the region's cool nights and wind. Lafage is a producer with broad holdings and modern cellar practice in the Roussillon; Tessellae sits in their range as an accessible old-vine blend that leans into structure and density rather than over-extraction. Taste-wise, expect ripe black cherry and plum overlaid with garrigue, black pepper and a stony minerality that comes from the area's schist and granite substrates.",
  "terroir_expression": "Côtes du Roussillon's Mediterranean climate — hot, dry summers with the Tramontane wind and greater diurnal range near the foothills of the Pyrenees — forces vines to root deep, concentrating phenolics. Schist and granite produce gritty mineral notes and firm tannins, while pockets of limestone soften acidity and add a saline lift; Tessellae reads as concentrated dark fruit with a saline-mineral streak and rosemary/tarragon herb notes because of that soil and climatic mix.",
  "vinification_summary": "Lafage typically uses low-yield old vines and controlled fermentations to preserve varietal fruit and structure; old-vine fruit naturally yields higher skin-to-juice ratios, which increases tannin and flavor concentration (this is why wines from old vines often taste denser). Expect standard red techniques: destemming/crushing, temperature-controlled fermentation to manage extraction, and modest barrel or concrete élevage to integrate tannins without masking regional aromatics.",

parsed.hook: Tessellae Old Vines is a Côtes du Roussillon red built from low-yield, old-vine fruit with a Mediterranean imprint: hot, dry summers, the drying Tramontane wind and soils of schist, granite and limestone across the appellation. That combination concentrates dark fruit and savory, mineral tannins — a workhorse Roussillon red that trades high-octane ripeness for layered, terroir-driven weight.
parsed.wine_summary: This bottling matters because it channels the identity of Côtes du Roussillon — sun-ripe Grenache/Carignan-driven character (grape varieties are not specified on the label) tempered by the region's cool nights and wind. Lafage is a producer with broad holdings and modern cellar practice in the Roussillon; Tessellae sits in their range as an accessible old-vine blend that leans into structure and density rather than over-extraction. Taste-wise, expect ripe black cherry and plum overlaid with garrigue, black pepper and a stony minerality that comes from the area's schist and granite substrates.
parsed.terroir_expression: Côtes du Roussillon's Mediterranean climate — hot, dry summers with the Tramontane wind and greater diurnal range near the foothills of the Pyrenees — forces vines to root deep, concentrating phenolics. Schist and granite produce gritty mineral notes and firm tannins, while pockets of limestone soften acidity and add a saline lift; Tessellae reads as concentrated dark fruit with a saline-mineral streak and rosemary/tarragon herb notes because of that soil and climatic mix.
parsed.vinification_summary: Lafage typically uses low-yield old vines and controlled fermentations to preserve varietal fruit and structure; old-vine fruit naturally yields higher skin-to-juice ratios, which increases tannin and flavor concentration (this is why wines from old vines often taste denser). Expect standard red techniques: destemming/crushing, temperature-controlled fermentation to manage extraction, and modest barrel or concrete élevage to integrate tannins without masking regional aromatics.

Nashville hot chicken (balanced heat level) with pickles and white bread — ripe fruit and acidity cool the heat while structure supports the spice.
Confit pork belly with lentils and mustard jus (bistro-fine) — the wine's mid-palate density counters the pork fat and the saline-mineral lift complements the lentils.
Piment d'Espelette-spiced Basque chicken with roasted peppers — bright red-fruit flavors and peppery spice in the wine dovetail with the dish's sweet-heat profile.

parsed.insider_take: Treat this as a food wine first: buy Tessellae when you need a robust, herbaceous red for rich, rustic dishes rather than a wine to sip solo for delicate aromatics. The real tradeoff is density versus finesse — you get concentrated old-vine fruit and savory tannin at a good price, but you won't find the layered precision of a single-vineyard Roussillon cuvée.
